title: Being counted
hookLine: showing up so a minyan can happen
tomorrow: Mr. Feld's in the hospital. visit and talk, or go and sweep?

cards: Seven in the morning, a small shul, and the group text says what it says too often: we have nine. Nine people can pray. What they can't do is say Kaddish, the mourner's prayer, or read from the Torah scroll in public.
Those wait for ten. So where does ten come from? Here's the odd part.
The Talmud finds it in the Torah's worst crowd: the spies who came back from Canaan and talked a whole people out of going in. God calls them, in the JPS 1917 translation, "this evil congregation."

teach.h: TWELVE SPIES, TEN WITH A BAD REPORT.
teach.b: Count the spies with the bad report. The Torah sends twelve, and two of them, Joshua and Caleb, disagree.
That leaves ten, and the Torah calls those ten a congregation, an edah. The Talmud, in tractate Megillah, links that word to another verse, where God is made holy among the children of Israel.
A congregation is ten, it reasons, so holiness in public needs ten. That ten is a minyan. Now the puzzle: why build a holy number on a bad crowd?
One answer some teachers give is that a congregation was never a club of saints.

teach.h: NOT SAINTS: PEOPLE WHO SHOW UP.
teach.b: It's people who show up, imperfect, and get counted. Who counts differs. In Orthodox synagogues, the ten are men past bar mitzvah; in egalitarian communities, women count as well.
Either way, the tenth person isn't an extra. The mourner standing there can't say Kaddish for a parent until somebody else walks in.

Something to tell a friend tonight: there's an old reluctance to count people by number, so some congregations count with a verse instead, a line from Psalms with ten Hebrew words, one word per person.
It asks God to save the people and bless them. Nobody is a number. Each one is a word in a blessing.

how: Many synagogues hold daily morning and evening services that need a minyan of ten for Kaddish and the Torah reading; members often sign up or get a call when a mourner needs the tenth person.

o: showing up so a congregation of ten can pray together
adding your name to a synagogue's membership list
the census once taken of all the tribes of Israel

games.q: where ten comes from — tap the pairs.

s: a minyan has to be ten especially devout people
the Talmud learns ten from the spies, 'this evil congregation'. a congregation is people who show up.
the mourner's Kaddish waits for a minyan of ten
nine can pray, but Kaddish and the public Torah reading wait for ten.
every synagogue counts the same people toward ten
Orthodox synagogues count men past bar mitzvah; egalitarian communities count women as well.

games.q: a weeknight, you're tired, and the shul text says: we have nine, and a mourner is here. what does your being there do?
o: it makes the tenth, so the mourner can say Kaddish.
not much: nine can say every prayer, just more quietly.
it mostly helps the shul's attendance numbers look good.
games.why: Kaddish waits for ten. the tenth person isn't an extra; being counted is what lets the mourner say it.

practice: Stand up where you are, feet planted, as if you just walked through the door and made it ten. Feel your weight on the floor; that's what showing up weighs.
Stay standing, and name one gathering this week where your being there could make the difference.

wordCard.voice: Being counted: showing up so something holy can happen. Ten make a congregation, and the tenth matters as much as the first.

orig.note: Hebrew: a count, a number; the quorum of ten for public prayer.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: be counted, because somewhere a mourner is waiting for ten. That's two days of community.

sources.ref: Numbers 13–14 (twelve spies; Joshua and Caleb dissent)
Babylonian Talmud Megillah 23b (ten learned from 'congregation', linked to Leviticus 22:32)
Mishnah Megillah 4:3 (what is not done with fewer than ten)
Psalm 28:9 (the ten-word verse used for counting); Babylonian Talmud Yoma 22b (reluctance to count people by number)
